title: RubSE: Why Self-Fixing UI Code Keeps Breaking What It Just Fixed
hook: A model told to make its screenshot match the design fixes one region and quietly wrecks another. RubSE names that failure — visual repair coupling — and fences each edit in with a rubric.
key_points: Visual repair coupling: one local code edit propagates through layout, style, and component dependencies, degrading regions that were already faithful.
That coupling makes naive test-time self-evolution unstable — later rounds can be worse than earlier ones.
RubSE turns visual feedback into a structured repair context: typed candidate rubrics, generated fresh each round.
Each round it picks one prioritized repair target and keeps past rubrics as history, discouraging repeated or over-broad rewrites.
Across six VLMs and three UI-to-code benchmarks it beat naive self-evolution in both final-round and best-round settings.
Analysis credits the gain to better recovery from severe regressions; stronger rubric generators can also guide weaker code improvers.
content_html: Vision-language models can turn a screenshot into working UI code, but letting them iterate on their own output is oddly fragile: round three is often worse than round two. Tianyi Xiong and colleagues (arXiv, August 2026) put a name to why. They call it visual repair coupling — because a page's layout, styling, and components are entangled, an edit aimed at one mismatched region ripples outward and breaks regions that already looked right.
extra_html: Their fix, RubSE, refuses to let the model free-associate about what to change. Each refinement round generates typed candidate rubrics from the visual feedback, selects a single prioritized repair target, and stores the rubrics already used as history — so revisions stay well-scoped and don't churn over the same ground. Across six VLMs and three UI-to-code benchmarks, the authors report it outperforming naive self-evolution in both final-round and best-round scoring, with steadier refinement trajectories. Their analysis attributes much of the gain to avoiding trajectory collapse: RubSE recovers from severe visual regressions where plain self-refinement spirals. A related finding is that a strong rubric generator can steer a weaker code improver, hinting the structured feedback, not just the editor model, is doing the work. Full paper and numbers at the arXiv link.

related.title: V-Rubrics: Grading a VLM's Answer Fact by Fact
related.hook: A single ungrounded object or misread chart value can sink an otherwise good answer — and a pass/fail reward can't tell you which part broke. V-Rubrics hands out partial credit per visual claim.

related.title: Anchored Self-Play for Code Repair
related.hook: Let a model train itself by writing bugs and fixing them, and you get a free difficulty curriculum — until it invents bugs no real codebase would produce. Anchored Self-Play keeps it honest.

flashcards.back_html: A local code edit propagates through layout, style, and component dependencies — so fixing one visual mismatch degrades regions of the render that were previously faithful.

flashcards.prompt: How does RubSE keep an iterative UI-to-code fix from sprawling?

choices.text: It generates typed rubrics, commits to one prioritized repair target per round, and keeps prior rubrics as history
It regenerates the whole page from scratch each round and keeps the best render
It freezes the CSS and only allows edits to the component tree

flashcards.explanation_html: Rubrics act as a structured visual-repair context: one scoped target per round, with history to discourage repeating or over-broadening edits.

flashcards.prompt: What does the paper's transfer result suggest about where the rubrics matter?
flashcards.back_html: A stronger rubric generator can hand effective visual-repair guidance to a weaker code improver — the feedback structure carries value independently of the model doing the editing.
